As we have already mentioned throughout the module, using GenAI in academic work does not change who is responsible for the work produced. You are responsible for the whole process: from how you decide to use GenAI for, to what you submit. 

Always keep in mind these five principles of academic integrity:
Be honest about how you use GenAI. Which platforms did you use? For what specific exercises? How did you evaluate the output?
Keep track of how you use AI for your academic work, even
to AI. Remember: the beginning is always yours, and the ending is always yours. Start with your own thinking and critically evaluate what GenAI
Ask yourself: 1) Are the core ideas and judgments in this assignment m

You remain fully responsible for the work you submit. You must ensure that your work is your own, verify the accuracy of information and references, and be able to explain and defend your arguments and conclusions.

c3.block-1.Text 1: C1 covered what GenAI is. C2 covered what it is to us. C3 covers the operational layer: how we actually interact with it. This is not a collection of prompt tips, but a framework built around one cycle.

c3.block-4.Text 1: A prompt is a text input given to GenAI to instruct a task. Research defines prompt engineering as "the skill of articulating a problem, its context, and the constraints of the desired solution to an AI assistant" (Federiakin et al., 2024).
c3.block-4.Text 3: . It is the act of defining what you want to do, what you expect, what process to follow, and under what conditions. Think of it as designing a virtual workspace where AI operates on your terms. To write a good prompt, you need to understand GenAI, but you also need to understand yourself: your task, your intention, your current stage, and your boundaries.

c3.block-5.Text 1: "Learning how to interact with AI is not unlike being someone who's really good at asking questions. Prompting AI is very similar. You can't just randomly ask a bunch of questions. Asking AI to be an assistant to you requires some expertise and artistry of how to prompt it."
c3.block-5.Text 2: — Jensen Huang, CEO of NVIDIA (Cleo Abram, "Huge Conversations", January 2025)

c3.block-6.Text 1: Six types of information AI uses to process a task

c3.block-7.Text 1: Research consistently shows that AI performs significantly better when certain types of information are clearly provided. The following six are the key components that support how AI processes and responds to your request.

c3.block-9.Text 4: . The more you specify the purpose, scope, context, and conditions of a task, the narrower AI's working space becomes.
c3.block-9.Text 5: AI interprets the task in the most generic way possible, based on the patterns that it has learned. Whether it matches your intent is left to chance.
c3.block-9.Text 6: Consensus: treated as baseline across all major prompt engineering surveys

c3.extra-0.Text 3: › C3 · How Do We Use AI?

c3.block-10.Text 4: . Setting a role is not a technique to boost AI accuracy — it is the act of deciding what position you want AI to occupy for this task.
c3.block-10.Text 5: AI generates output that aligns with the general instruction to act as a "helpful assistant."
c3.block-10.Text 6: Evidence: no measurable accuracy improvement on benchmarks (Zheng et al., 2024 EMNLP; 162 personas, 4 LLM families). Effective as a tone and framing tool.
c3.block-10.Emphasis 1: the perspective from which AI should approach the task

c3.block-11.Text 4: . When you give AI a complex task all at once, it becomes harder to identify at which step something went wrong.
c3.block-11.Text 5: the model determines for itself which intermediate steps are needed based on your prompt. These may not align with the approach you had in mind.
c3.block-11.Text 6: Evidence: Least-to-Most prompting showed 83.5pp gain on compositional benchmarks (Zhou et al., 2022 ICLR)
c3.block-11.Emphasis 1: the steps involved in completing a task

c3.block-12.Text 4: . Creating an example forces you to check: do I actually know what I want? Modern models can also infer the type of output you expect from your instructions without examples, but this requires them to make more assumptions themselves.
c3.block-12.Text 5: the model has less information about the format and level of detail you expect in the output.
c3.block-12.Text 6: Evidence: established in Brown et al. (2020, NeurIPS) GPT-3 paper. Few-shot CoT scored highest in Schulhoff et al. benchmarks.
c3.block-12.Emphasis 1: what the desired output should look like, illustrated by one or more examples

c3.block-13.Text 4: . By asking AI to work through the analysis in separate steps, you can evaluate each step individually.
c3.block-13.Text 5: You may receive only a conclusion, making it harder to assess what that conclusion is based on.
c3.block-13.Text 6: Evidence: Wei et al. (2022, NeurIPS) GSM8K 18% → 58%. However, effects are limited outside math/symbolic reasoning (Sprague et al., 2024).
c3.block-13.Emphasis 1: the steps in which a complex task should be carried out

c3.block-14.Text 4: . The same content, presented as a table, a list, a single sentence, or a set of questions, changes how you can use the output afterward. Specifying the format is therefore not just a convenience: it determines how the output can be used in your workflow.
c3.block-14.Text 5: AI falls back on its default format (usually long paragraphs).
c3.block-14.Text 6: Revisited in Section 3 (Integrate) from the integration strategy perspective.
c3.block-14.Emphasis 1: how the output should be presented

c3.block-16.Text 1: If you think through these components before prompting, you stay in control of the task. If you skip them, AI fills them in for you, and because its output looks plausible, you may not realize decisions were made without you. Having your own ideas about these components before you let AI work is what we call proactive GenAI use.

c3.block-18.List text 1: What exactly am I trying to do right now?
c3.block-18.List text 2: What is the purpose of this task?
c3.block-18.List text 4: Which stage of my project does this task belong to?

c3.block-19.List text 1: What perspective should AI operate from?
c3.block-19.List text 3: What tone and level of response do I need?

c3.block-20.List text 1: Can I break this task into smaller units?
c3.block-20.List text 2: Am I trying to ask for too much at once?
c3.block-20.List text 3: What order should the sub-tasks follow?

c3.block-21.List text 1: Do I know what the desired output looks like?
c3.block-21.List text 3: If I can't make an example, do I actually know what I want?

c3.block-22.List text 1: What steps does the analysis required for this task involve?
c3.block-22.List text 2: What steps should AI go through?
c3.block-22.List text 3: Do I need to see the intermediate process?

c3.block-23.List text 1: What format do I need to actually use it?
c3.block-23.List text 3: Is this format easy to integrate into my workflow?

c3.block-24.Text 1: Based on these components, you build your prompt.

c3.block-25.Text 6: I am currently working on _______. This task is part of _______.
c3.block-25.Text 12: Respond in the form of a _______.
c3.block-25.Text 14: Here is an example of what I want: _______.

c3.block-26.Heading 1: Output is not an answer — it is a proposal

c3.block-27.Text 1: What AI gives you is not a final answer but a
c3.block-27.Text 2: : a possible structure, wording, comparison, or interpretation. Output is material to review, not material to directly adopt.
c3.block-27.Text 3: This connects directly to what you learned in C1. GenAI output is statistically likely, not factually verified. The model generates text based on patterns and probabilities, without checking for itself whether the content is correct. It is limited by the information it was trained on and the information you provide. That is why you need your own knowledge to critically evaluate the output.

c3.block-28.Text 1: Four steps: Read → Question → Verify → Decide

c3.block-30.List text 1: Is this a response to what I requested?
c3.block-30.List text 2: What structure did AI use? (list, paragraphs, table, etc.)
c3.block-30.List text 3: What overall claim or direction is it taking?

c3.block-31.List text 3: Are any parts overly general or vague?
c3.block-31.List text 4: Does the output include claims I can't verify?
c3.block-31.List text 5: Did the output stay within my requested scope?

c3.block-32.List text 1: If facts, references, or figures are included — can I verify them against the original source?
c3.block-32.List text 2: Does the output match the scope of my request?
c3.block-32.List text 3: Can I explain this content myself?
c3.block-32.List text 4: Does this output reflect my intent and context?

c3.block-33.List text 1: Which insights from the output are useful for my own further development, and which should I reject?
c3.block-33.List text 2: What do I need to change or develop further in my own work?

c3.block-34.Heading 1: How AI output enters your work

c3.block-35.Text 1: Integration does not start after you receive the output — it starts at the prompting stage. The moment you decide on the format in which you want to receive the output, you are already influencing how easily you can critically evaluate it and use it responsibly in your further workflow.
c3.block-35.Text 2: "Compare these papers" may produce paragraphs that can easily become mixed up with your own text. "Make a comparison table" keeps the output separate from your text and makes the information verifiable cell by cell. Choosing the output format is not a convenience — it helps you keep AI-generated output

c3.block-36.Text 1: Carries the highest risk of becoming mixed with your own writing and of unintentionally adopting AI-generated wording. Avoid this format when working on texts that you are expected to write yourself.
c3.block-36.Table text 4: Verifiable cell by cell. Keeps AI output clearly separate from your own text.
c3.block-36.Table text 6: Serves as a thinking prompt. You use the questions to think and write further yourself.
c3.block-36.Table text 8: Presents a single claim — easy to assess and verify separately.
c3.block-36.Table text 10: Provides possible concepts or search directions that you can evaluate and then develop yourself.
c3.block-36.Table text 12: Makes a possible structure visible that you can access before continuing your own work.

c3.block-39.Text 2: Break the output into units that can be judged independently. Rows for tables, items for lists, claims for paragraphs.

c3.block-40.Text 2: Assign a tag to each unit:
c3.block-40.List text 1: accurate, aligns with my intention, and is useful as input for my own further development
c3.block-40.List text 2: the direction is right, but the content needs adjustment
c3.block-40.List text 3: incorrect, outside scope, or something I cannot verify

c3.block-41.Text 1: Execute — Take action based on each tag
c3.block-41.List text 1: use the insight or information as input for your own work; check the original source and formulate it yourself.
c3.block-41.List text 2: determine what needs to change; return to the original source or prompt again.
c3.block-41.List text 3: do not use it; note why in one sentence.

c3.block-42.Text 1: Review — Look at the bigger picture
c3.block-42.Text 2: After integration, consider the work as a whole:
c3.block-42.List text 1: Does this reflect my own thinking?
c3.block-42.List text 2: Did I write the final text myself without adopting AI-generated wording?
c3.block-42.List text 3: Can I explain and defend every part of it?

c3.block-43.Text 2: Based on the Author Checklist from Cheng, Calhoun, & Reedy (2025). Advances in Simulation, 10, 22.
c3.block-43.List text 1: Are the core ideas and judgments in this work my own?
c3.block-43.List text 2: Did I write the final text myself without adopting AI-generated phrasing?
c3.block-43.List text 3: Can I explain and defend every part of this work?
c3.block-43.List text 4: Can I transparently disclose how AI was used?

c3.block-44.Text 1: Use GenAI responsibly during your study work, make sure you adhere to the ESSB principles and Guidelines.

c3.block-46.Text 1: The way you structure and format a prompt can have a significant impact on GenAI's performance. Research shows that formatting changes alone can lead to differences in accuracy up to 76 percentage points for some models and tasks (Sclar et al., ICLR 2024). Two common structuring formats are Markdown and XML.

c3.block-48.Text 5: for lists — intuitive and easy for humans to read. XML uses explicit opening and closing tags, which models parse more precisely. XML is the only delimiter format recommended by all three major providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google), making it advantageous for complex prompts.

c3.block-50.Text 5: [What specifically needs to be done? Specify the goal, context, and task]
c3.block-50.Text 8: [The situation this task sits in. Current stage, background, materials]
c3.block-50.Text 11: [What should AI NOT do? Scope limits. Conditions to respect]
c3.block-50.Text 14:
[The steps involved in completing the task]
1. ...
2. ...
3. ...
c3.block-50.Text 17: [Shape, length, and structure of the output]

c3.block-52.Table text 4: 50–100 words (summary, factual question): Keep the prompt short and include only the information needed for the task.
c3.block-52.Table text 6: 150–300 words (analysis, comparison, structured output): Add relevant context, constraints, and the desired output format.
c3.block-52.Table text 8: 300–500 words (multi-step reasoning, detailed generation): Make the different components and steps of the task explicit.
c3.block-52.Table text 10: Consider breaking the task into multiple steps or prompts, allowing you to check and adjust the output along the way.

c3.block-54.Text 5: "Please", "thank you", and "if you don't mind" are unnecessary and can reduce performance (Dobariya & Kumar, 2025).
c3.block-54.Text 9: Place key instructions at the edges
c3.block-54.Text 10: Put the most important instructions at the very beginning or very end of your prompt, countering the "Lost in the Middle" effect (Liu et al., 2024).
